newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British retail sales herald consumer boom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British retail sales herald consumer boom.

text.p: British retail sales rose a hefty one percent in August and 4.4 percent on the year, official data showed on Wednesday, suggesting Britain's consumers are queueing up to spend their money.
The sales figures comfortably exceeded market expectations and, with a host of retailers reporting better trading conditions, Britain's high streets appear awash with activity.
"The simplest story is the correct one. Sales are buoyant," said Kevin Gardiner, UK economist at Morgan Stanley.
Not only did retail sales show a strong annual rise, the three-month rate of increase was the strongest since August 1988, the Office for National Statistics said.
That will be welcome news for the Conservative government, which faces elections by May 1997 and badly lags the opposition Labour Party in opinion polls.
A Treasury spokesman, reacting to the sales figures, said the British economy was growing at the most sustainable rate of any major European country.
Evidence from Britain's major retailers in the past week has certainly supported the buoyant sales picture.

On Wednesday, supermarket group Tesco Plc reported a 10.7 percent increase in first half pre-tax profits to 321 million pounds ($499.3 million), while clothes retailer Next Plc saw its pre-tax profits in the first half of the year jump almost 27 percent to 56 million.
Last week department store group The John Lewis Partnership said sales for a recent six week period were up a bumper 17.3 percent year-on-year.
Analysts said August's sales data confirmed survey evidence from groups such as the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) and British Retail Consortium (BRC).
For some time, they have pointed to robust increases in consumer spending, yet official figures registered a 0.6 percent drop in sales volumes in July. Now, they have moved into line.

"The improvement in the trend supports all the anecdotal evidence and is suggesting the consumer sector is finally starting to move ahead," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic advisor at BankAmerica.

The BRC's August sales survey showed retail sales values rose 6.9 percent on an annual basis in August, while the last CBI distributive trades survey showed the largest balance of firms reporting an increase in sales since 1988.
Some analysts said retail sales may be less robust than the bald figures suggest. British consumers remain ultra-price conscious, they said, and will only part with money when the price is right.
But Gardiner said the notion that sales were only rising as prices were squeezed was a red herring.
The official data released on Wednesday showed overall retail sales were up 6.0 percent from a year earlier in value terms. So it is not just volumes that are increasing.
"And given the supporting evidence of a housing recovery, spiralling mortgage lending and monetary and credit growth, it's all going one way," Gardiner said.
All that adds up to a fast-closing door on the hopes for further interest rate cuts.

Minutes of the July 30 monetary meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George, showed the central bank chief asked for a quarter-point interest rate rise to 6.00 percent.
He said the latest economic evidence showed a pickup in consumer-led demand. August's sales data certainly support that.
But with a general election looming, an interest rate rise would be seen as political poison.
"(Clarke's) tactics now seem clear -- to hold out against a rise in interest rates as long as possible," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. ($1=.6428 Pound)
